chunks: I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) saying: 'Whilst I was in the tawaf (circumambulation), suddenly a man grabbed my garment, and he was Abbad ibn Kathir al-Basri.
He said: O Ja'far ibn Muhammad! You are wearing the likes of these clothes, while you are in this sacred place, along with the rank you hold from Ali (peace be upon him)?

So I said: It is a Furqubi (Egyptian linen) garment I bought for one dinar. Ali (peace be upon him) lived in an era when what he wore was appropriate for that time, and if I were to wear the likes of that attire in our time, the people would say: This one is a show-off like Abbad.'

key_terms.الطواف: Tawaf — the ritual circumambulation of the Ka'ba, performed counterclockwise seven times; one of the essential rites of Hajj and Umra
key_terms.المكان: Al-makan — here meaning spiritual rank or proximity in lineage to Imam Ali, not merely the physical location
key_terms.فرقبي: Furqubi — a type of fine Egyptian linen cloth, prized for its quality; relatively expensive but not extravagant
key_terms.مراء: Mura'in — one who practices riya', showing off religious devotion or asceticism for social approval; a major spiritual vice in Islamic ethics condemned in both the Quran and hadith

ai.seo_question: What did Imam Sadiq say about wearing fine clothes during tawaf?
ai.summary: This hadith narrates an encounter during the tawaf (circumambulation of the Kaaba at Mecca) in which Abbad ibn Kathir al-Basri, a well-known Sunni ascetic from Basra known for his ostentatious piety and coarse dress, challenges Imam al-Sadiq (AS) about wearing fine Egyptian linen cloth near the sacred site. Imam al-Sadiq responds with a nuanced and historically grounded principle: the appropriateness of dress is context-sensitive and era-dependent. He explains that while Imam Ali's austere style was suited to his turbulent era of war and poverty, if the Imam were to adopt such conspicuous austerity in Abbasid-era Medina, it would become a form of riya' (ostentation or showing off), since people would interpret it as deliberate religious display. The hadith teaches that avoiding both luxury and performative austerity is the mark of genuine piety.
